title: Salmon vs. sardines: omega-3, protein, and calories

seo.title: Salmon vs. sardines: omega-3, protein, calories
seo.meta_description: Salmon and sardines are both rich in protein and EPA+DHA. Salmon usually has more long-chain omega-3 per 100 g; bone-in sardines stand out for calcium.
seo.search_intent: Compare salmon and sardines for omega-3, protein, fat and calories using equal weights and clearly defined forms.

excerpt: Salmon and sardines are surprisingly close in protein and calories. Both provide EPA and DHA; cooked Atlantic salmon can land around 2 grams EPA+DHA per 100 grams, while canned sardines are often around 1.4 grams, depending on species and product.
content_html:
Salmon and sardines look very different on the plate, yet both deliver substantial protein and meaningful amounts of EPA and DHA. The useful question is not which fish wins permanently, but what each contributes in the form you actually eat.

A practical comparison per 100 g

NutrientCooked Atlantic salmonCanned sardines, drained
Calories~180–210~185–210
Protein~20–23 g~24–25 g
Fat~10–13 g~10–12 g
EPA+DHA~1.8–2.2 g~1.3–1.5 g

NIH lists 1.83 g EPA+DHA in 3 oz of cooked farmed Atlantic salmon and 1.19 g in 3 oz of canned sardines in tomato sauce, drained. Converted to 100 g, that is roughly 2.15 g versus 1.40 g.

Sardines can edge higher in protein

Many drained sardine products provide roughly 24–25 g protein/100 g because the canned fish is relatively concentrated. Cooked salmon commonly sits around 20–23 g/100 g. Across a 4-ounce serving, that is roughly 27–28 g protein from sardines versus about 23–26 g from salmon.

Calories can be much closer than expected

Fatty salmon and drained sardines can both fall around 190–210 calories per 100 g. Canning medium matters: sardines that retain more oil can be higher, while a well-drained tomato-sauce product can land differently.

Salmon often has more EPA+DHA, but sardines are still concentrated

Using the NIH examples, salmon provides about 0.75 g more EPA+DHA per 100 g, roughly 54% more. Sardines still easily clear 1 g EPA+DHA per 100 g in many references.

Edible bones give sardines a separate advantage

When the soft bones are eaten, canned sardines can provide several hundred milligrams of calcium per 100 g. A boneless salmon fillet contains only a small fraction of that amount. The difference comes from eating the mineralized bones, not from a special property of sardine flesh.

Sodium, species, and packing liquid matter

Canned sardine sodium depends on added salt and sauce. Fresh salmon is naturally much lower in sodium before seasoning. Omega-3 content also changes with salmon species, wild versus farmed production, and feed.

The useful takeaway

Both salmon and sardines are strong protein and marine omega-3 foods. Atlantic salmon generally provides more EPA+DHA per 100 g; canned sardines can provide slightly more protein and dramatically more calcium when the bones are eaten. For calories, check the specific product and packing oil.

faq.question: Which has more omega-3, salmon or sardines?
faq.answer: In NIH examples, cooked Atlantic salmon is about 2.15 g EPA+DHA per 100 g versus roughly 1.40 g for drained canned sardines in tomato sauce.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: Canned sardines often provide about 24–25 g/100 g versus roughly 20–23 g in cooked salmon.

faq.question: Why are canned sardines high in calcium?
faq.answer: Their softened bones are usually edible, and those bones contain much of the calcium.
